body: The dishwasher downstairs finishes its cycle and clicks twice, and a man of thirty-four, lying on his back with one hand flat on his chest, hears it and carries on counting. He has counted to sixty four times. It is twenty past four; the alarm goes at half past five, so there is no point now, and he knows there is no point. He has already established, in some detail, that the meeting at eleven will be fine, that nobody is going to say anything, and that the thing he sent on Friday was correct. None of it has made the slightest difference to his heart.
He is not worrying about the meeting. He settled the meeting hours ago. Whatever is going on in his chest was never listening to the argument, which is the part almost nobody says out loud.

Be anxious for nothing. It is among the most quoted lines in the New Testament, it is on a great many fridge magnets, and it is among the most damaging things in the book when it is quoted on its own, which is nearly always.

In English, on its own, it lands as an instruction about how to feel, and nobody has ever successfully followed an instruction about how to feel. Take the grammar seriously. Give, forgive, visit the sick, tell the truth when it costs you — every one of those names an action, and a person can do the action badly, or reluctantly, or with the wrong face on, and still have done it. Feel differently names no action at all. There is no first step in it. So the man on his back at twenty past four has a command with no way of obeying it, and the only thing available to him is to fail.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air today. One of the numbers, HM 394.80, is assigned to a station called Anxious No More. It is in build, not yet on air, still silent.

The name was an argument before it was a name, and the argument is the whole remit of that frequency. Be anxious for nothing is not an instruction to feel differently. It is an instruction about where to put the thing. That is a claim about grammar rather than willpower, and it can be checked against the rest of the sentence. Holding a number for that distinction is not good business — a station declining to promise the outcome its own name suggests has given away the easiest thing it had to sell — but the alternative is to leave the misreading in circulation, and the misreading is what does the harm.

What the half-verse produces, handed over warmly at the wrong moment, is a second problem stacked on the first. The person is anxious. Now they are also disobedient, and the disobedience is evidence for what they already suspected about themselves, which is that other people manage this and they do not. Anyone given that verse during a genuinely bad stretch knows the exact shape of the silence afterwards. They did not argue. They said thank you. And they added one more item to the list of things about them that would need explaining.

Read the whole of it and the machinery is different. Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known unto God. The verb carrying the weight is not stop. It is make known. That is a transfer, available to a person in the middle of the state rather than a condition for getting out of it. And what is promised at the end is not the absence of anxiety but a peace described as passing understanding — a strange thing to promise unless the circumstances producing the anxiety are expected to still be there.
The verse is not a cure. It never claimed to be one, and reading it as one is what has done the damage.

The usual alternative is reassurance, and reassurance deserves a fair hearing, because it is kind and it is often correct. The meeting will be fine. The test will come back clear. Nobody thinks that about you. All of it may be true and none of it holds, because reassurance operates on the content and the content is not the engine. Answer one and it moves. It will be the meeting until the meeting is settled, then the money, then a noise the car is making. Anybody who has spent a decade in that loop has worked out that the topic is interchangeable, which is a lonely thing to know.
You cannot argue with something that was never an argument.

A woman of fifty-eight, signed off work since March, stands in her hallway at twenty past nine on a Tuesday with her coat on and her keys in her hand. The shop is nine minutes away. She has been standing long enough that her hand has gone warm around the keys. She goes back to the kitchen, puts the radio on, turns it up a little louder than she would if she were staying, and leaves it playing to the empty room. Then she goes out. It takes twenty-two minutes and she buys milk and a birthday card. None of the walk was pleasant. She does the same thing on the Thursday.

Nothing in that was calm being delivered. Anxiety narrows a house to one point and holds it there. Something audible carrying on elsewhere is evidence, at the level of the ear rather than the argument, that the house has other rooms.

That is a small mechanism and it is right to say so, because it will not be enough for a great many people, and the ones for whom it is not enough are usually the ones told hardest that it ought to be. Some of this is a body: a thyroid, a medication, a debt that is real, a house that is genuinely unsafe. None of that is touched by anything coming out of a speaker. A station cannot tell a hard fortnight from an illness, and should never be asked to try.

But notice what a frequency cannot do, and how rare that is in a house. It has no view about whether you are improving. It does not ask how you have been, does not remember what you said last time, cannot be disappointed and cannot be relieved. Everybody else under that roof has a stake in your recovery, which is love, and which also makes every ordinary conversation quietly an assessment. The thing playing in the kitchen is the only object in the building with no opinion about your progress. That is not a shortfall in the offer. It is the offer.

So the command is not the cure and the station is not the treatment, and neither is being proposed as one. What is proposed is smaller and more defensible: that a misread half-verse has been used to make anxious people ashamed, that the whole verse asks for a transfer rather than a feeling, and that a thing which plays without asking anything is one of the few objects in a bad week that costs nothing to be near. The state may well still be there tomorrow. Nothing here promises otherwise.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing, so here is the part that is not.

The band carries four kinds of programming and it is worth knowing they are there. There is music, which is most of it. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on with children in the room. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them. A block of numbers is held for hard stretches — When Faith Feels Hard, After the Storm, The Mended Place, and the Anxious No More frequency named above — all assigned, in build, not yet on air.

What is on air, and what I would put on at twenty past nine in a hallway, is HM 301.90 — Radiant Stones Concerts. It carries concert recordings: rooms of people already singing, caught while they were doing it. That matters here for one specific reason. Most worship recording is made to be joined, and joining is a demand — stand, lift your hands, sing, mean it — and a demand is the thing an anxious person has least capacity for. A concert is a room you are at the back of. The work is being done by several hundred people who do not know you are there and will carry on whether or not you make a sound. Nothing on HM 301.90 requires you to produce anything. You are simply in the building.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So put HM 301.90 on this afternoon while you are doing something else, and then leave it alone. Do not use it as a test. Do not sit down in a week to work out whether you are calmer; that turns the one object in the house with no view on your progress into another thing keeping score. Let it run in a room you are not in. Then go and do the nine minutes to the shop, or do not, and know the radio is not marking you either way and will still be playing when you get back.
